blogs.title: When the Endoscopy is Normal: Red Flags for Neurogenic Dysphagia
blogs.description: This post explores the clinical challenge of a patient with recurrent choking episodes on both solids and liquids despite multiple normal laryngoscopies and endoscopies. It discusses why clinicians should pivot from a mechanical/gastrointestinal focus to a neurological evaluation when 'unexplained' dysphagia persists, specifically highlighting the role of brainstem compression and lower cranial nerve involvement.

blogs.title: The Silent Desaturator: Understanding Acquired Central Hypoventilation
blogs.description: A deep dive into the physiology of 'Ondine’s Curse' in the context of structural brain pathology. This post explains the distinction between voluntary and automatic breathing, why some patients can maintain voluntary ventilation while failing automatically during sleep or distraction, and the fascinating concept of 'interoception failure'—why the patient may desaturate to dangerous levels without feeling 'air hunger.'

blogs.title: The Diagnostic Time Machine: The Value of Retrospective Imaging Review
blogs.description: This blog post discusses the 'hidden' history of the patient, where a 14-year-old CT scan provided the missing piece of the puzzle. It advocates for a systematic review of historical imaging in complex cases where the current clinical presentation is refractory to standard workups, illustrating how easily structural malformations can be overlooked in an acute or unrelated setting.

blogs.title: Beyond the Headache: Atypical Presentations of Chiari Malformation
blogs.description: While occipital headaches are a cardinal symptom of Chiari Malformation Type I (CMI), this post looks at the more nuanced and atypical presentations, such as vertex allodynia and 'burning vertex syndrome.' It discusses the spectrum of CMI, distinguishing between asymptomatic anatomical variants and symptomatic malformations that require intervention.

blogs.title: The Illusion of Mildness: Pitfalls of Type III Polysomnography
blogs.description: This post addresses a common pitfall in sleep medicine: the discrepancy between a 'mild' Apnea-Hypopnea Index (AHI) and severe clinical symptoms. It explains how the absence of EEG monitoring in Type III studies can lead to the significant underestimation of central events, particularly when total recording time includes periods of wakefulness.
